test_title: RRB NTPC (UG) CBT-I Official Paper (Held On: 28 Aug, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: Which Fundamental Right was removed from the Indian Constitution by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to Property**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **44th Amendment Act of 1978** removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution.
 
• Before the amendment, the Right to Property was enshrined under **Article 19(1)(f)** and Article 31.
 
• Post the amendment, the Right to Property was made a **legal right** under Article 300A of the Constitution.
 
• The change was implemented to address challenges related to land acquisition for developmental purposes and to reduce litigation.
 
• The Right to Property is no longer enforceable through writ petitions, unlike Fundamental Rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, providing essential rights to citizens.
 
• They include rights such as Equality, Freedom, Protection against exploitation, Freedom of religion, Cultural and educational rights, and Constitutional remedies.
 
• These rights are enforceable by courts and protect citizens against arbitrary actions by the state.
 
 
 
• **Article 300A:**
 
 
• It states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by authority of law.
 
• Article 300A falls under Part XII of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Right to Property is now a statutory right, meaning it can be regulated by legislation.
 
 
 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978:**
 
 
• This amendment was introduced under the leadership of Prime Minister Morarji Desai.
 
• It aimed to balance individual rights with public welfare and economic development.
 
• Alongside the removal of the Right to Property, it also introduced safeguards against misuse of emergency powers.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• Unlike Fundamental Rights, legal rights like the Right to Property cannot be challenged directly in the Supreme Court through writ petitions.
 
• Legal rights are subject to regulation and limitation by the legislature.
